gates.title: Grade 9 motion rates, graphs, constant acceleration and circular speed

canonical_concepts.statement: Average rates are formed from total path or displacement over the same total elapsed time, not by blindly averaging listed speeds.
The familiar kinematic equations are exact only on an interval where acceleration is constant.
On a position-time graph, interval slope gives average velocity; on a velocity-time graph, interval slope gives average acceleration.
Uniform circular motion has constant speed v = 2 pi r / T while its velocity direction changes continuously.

validity_conditions: One finite interval with a positive elapsed time.
Average velocity requires a declared signed displacement convention.
Constant-acceleration relations are used only on intervals where one acceleration value describes the whole interval.
Graph-slope relations use two coordinates from the same graph and one declared axis convention.
Uniform circular speed uses one complete circular path of radius r completed in positive period T.
The graphical derivation treats displacement as signed velocity-time area over one constant-acceleration interval.

reasoning_sequence.action: Form the total path length and signed displacement over the same interval.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Both averages must refer to the same elapsed interval.

reasoning_sequence.action: Divide each total by the common positive elapsed time.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Rate over an interval is total change measure divided by elapsed time.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Average speed is always the arithmetic mean of the listed speeds.
misconceptions.counterexample: Equal-distance legs at unequal speeds spend unequal times at the two speeds.
misconceptions.repair: Use total distance divided by total time unless equal time weighting is explicitly given.

gates.title: Average and instantaneous mechanical power

canonical_concepts.statement: Power is a rate of energy transfer; an interval average and an instantaneous rate answer different questions.

relations.meaning: Average power is work transferred over a positive elapsed interval.

symbols.meaning: Average power
Net work transferred over the interval
Positive elapsed interval

conditions: Delta t > 0.
W is the net work assigned to the chosen system over that same interval.

relations.meaning: Instantaneous mechanical power is the signed force component along velocity times instantaneous speed.

symbols.meaning: Instantaneous power
Signed component of force along the instantaneous velocity direction
Instantaneous speed

conditions: F_parallel carries the sign of the force component along or opposite the velocity direction.

validity_conditions: Average power uses one positive interval.
Instantaneous power uses quantities evaluated at the same instant.

reasoning_sequence.action: Decide whether the request is an interval average or an instantaneous rate.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: The two relations use different information.

reasoning_sequence.action: Evaluate the matching relation with a consistent work or force-velocity sign.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Sign distinguishes transfer into versus out of the mechanical account.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Objects that receive the same work must have the same power.
misconceptions.counterexample: The same work delivered in half the time has twice the average power.
misconceptions.repair: Keep total transfer and transfer rate as separate quantities.

problem_families.title: Compare equal work delivered over unequal times or changing instantaneous rates
hidden_invariants: Equal total work does not imply equal power.

gates.title: Newton's second law for net force and acceleration

canonical_concepts.statement: For a fixed positive mass, net force and acceleration are directed together and linked by F_net = m a.

relations.meaning: The vector net external force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration.

symbols.meaning: Net external force along the declared one-dimensional axis
Mass of the chosen body
Acceleration along the same declared axis

conditions: F_net and a refer to the same chosen body.
All signed components use one declared axis.

Use one inertial frame for the Grade 9 relation.
Mass is positive and treated as constant over the interval.

reasoning_sequence.action: Choose one body and one signed axis, then sum only external forces acting on that body.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Newton's second law applies to the net external force on one chosen body.

reasoning_sequence.action: Set the signed net force equal to mass times signed acceleration.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: REL-NEWTON-SECOND-LAW owns the quantitative relation.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Acceleration points in the direction of the largest individual force rather than the net force.
misconceptions.counterexample: Equal opposite forces can both be large while net force and acceleration are zero.
misconceptions.repair: Sum signed external forces first, then use the direction of F_net.

gates.title: Bounded friction and connected-body constraints

canonical_concepts.statement: Static friction supplies the tangential force required by a no-slip state only up to a limiting magnitude; the maximum is not the default value.
A common acceleration or string-length relation is justified by an active physical constraint, not by the mere presence of multiple bodies.
Uniform tension and fixed-length kinematics are consequences of an explicitly declared ideal string/pulley model and its geometry.

relations.meaning: For a contact that remains static, the static-friction magnitude adjusts to the value required by the tangential dynamics up to the limiting value mu_s N; equality applies only at impending slip.

symbols.meaning: Signed static friction force along the contact tangent
Coefficient of static friction for the contact model
Normal contact-force magnitude obtained from the actual perpendicular dynamics

conditions: The surfaces are in contact and have no relative sliding during the state being tested.
N is obtained from the actual free-body dynamics, not assumed to equal mg.
Static friction opposes the impending relative slip direction.
Equality |f_s| = mu_s N is used only at impending slip.

relations.meaning: Once relative sliding at the contact is established, the bounded dry-sliding model uses kinetic-friction magnitude mu_k N, directed opposite the relative sliding.

symbols.meaning: Signed kinetic friction force along the contact tangent
Coefficient of kinetic friction for the declared contact model
Normal contact-force magnitude from the actual perpendicular dynamics

conditions: Relative sliding between the two surfaces is established.
N is obtained from the actual free-body dynamics.
The friction direction opposes the relative sliding at the contact.
The simple dry-sliding coefficient model is being used.

relations.meaning: When an active connection keeps the relative separation of bodies A and B fixed along one shared coordinate and both use the same positive sense, their acceleration components along that coordinate are equal.

symbols.meaning: Acceleration component of body A along the declared shared coordinate
Acceleration component of body B along the same positive coordinate sense

conditions: The connection/contact actively keeps the relevant relative separation fixed.
Both acceleration components use the same coordinate direction and sign convention.
The constraint has not gone slack, separated, or otherwise ceased to apply.

relations.meaning: For one taut massless ideal string, with any direction-changing pulley/support treated as frictionless and massless in this bounded model, the tension magnitude is uniform throughout that same string.

symbols.meaning: Tension magnitude in the string segment acting on body A
Tension magnitude in the same string segment acting on body B
Common ideal-string tension magnitude

conditions: The same taut string connects the stated segments.
The string is massless and inextensible in the ideal model.
Any pulley/redirection used here is frictionless and massless and only changes string direction.
No nonideal feature is introduced that would require different tension magnitudes.

relations.expression: y_A + y_B = L_free = constant; a_A + a_B = 0
relations.meaning: For one taut inextensible string over one fixed ideal pulley, with both coordinates measured away from the pulley along the two straight segments, the variable segment lengths sum to a constant and the signed accelerations sum to zero.

symbols.meaning: Straight string-segment length/coordinate from fixed pulley to body A, positive away from the pulley
Straight string-segment length/coordinate from fixed pulley to body B, positive away from the pulley
Constant total of the two variable straight segments

Acceleration of B along positive y_B

conditions: There is one fixed pulley and one taut inextensible string.
Only the two declared straight segments change length; the wrapped/fixed portions are constant.
Both coordinates are measured away from the pulley along their local string segments.
The pulley itself does not translate.

validity_conditions: Choose body boundaries and coordinate directions before writing force or constraint equations.
Obtain the normal reaction from the actual perpendicular dynamics.
Use a static-friction equality only at impending slip; use the kinetic relation only after relative sliding is established.
Apply common-acceleration, equal-tension, and fixed-string-length relations only while their declared connection/model assumptions hold.
The fixed-pulley relation is restricted to one fixed pulley and one taut inextensible string with two changing straight segments.

reasoning_sequence.action: Choose the body or system boundary and declare coordinates.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Force ownership and acceleration signs depend on that choice.

reasoning_sequence.action: For friction, determine N and the no-slip friction requirement before selecting the static or kinetic relation.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: The coefficient relation depends on the contact state and actual normal reaction.

reasoning_sequence.action: For connected bodies, state the active separation/string constraint before equating accelerations or tensions.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Constraint equations are consequences of the physical model, not generic multi-body shortcuts.

reasoning_sequence.action: Check that the chosen relation still holds at the stated boundary case.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Slip, separation, slack, nonideal pulleys, or changed geometry invalidate different parts of the model.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Friction always equals a coefficient times the normal force.
misconceptions.counterexample: A static contact with zero tangential demand has zero friction even though mu_s N is positive.
misconceptions.repair: Solve the no-slip friction requirement first and compare it with the static limit.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any connected bodies can be assigned the same acceleration.
misconceptions.counterexample: Opposite ends of one fixed-pulley string have opposite signed accelerations when both coordinates point away from the pulley.
misconceptions.repair: Derive the kinematic relation from the active connection and coordinate convention.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every rope/pulley arrangement has equal tension everywhere.
misconceptions.counterexample: A frictional pulley or massive rope can require different tensions.
misconceptions.repair: State the ideal string/redirection assumptions before using one tension magnitude.

gates.title: Accelerating-frame observer choice, apparent weight, and hanging-bob transfer

canonical_concepts.statement: A scale measures the support/normal force, not mass or gravitational force; in an inertial vertical description the normal force changes with acceleration while mg remains the gravitational force.

When Newton's second law is written in a frame accelerating with a_frame, a pseudo-force -m a_frame is added as a frame-dependent modelling term; it is not a new physical interaction or a Newton-III partner.
An inertial-frame description and a consistently written accelerating-frame description of the same event must agree on observable quantities such as scale reading and string direction.

relations.meaning: For a person that remains in contact with a horizontal scale in an inertial ground frame, with upward positive and g the positive magnitude of gravitational acceleration, the signed vertical force balance is N - m g = m a_y.

symbols.meaning: Upward normal/support force exerted by the scale on the person
Person mass
Positive magnitude of gravitational acceleration
Person vertical acceleration, positive upward

conditions: The ground frame is treated as inertial and the positive vertical direction is upward.
The person remains in contact with the scale, so N >= 0.
The person and scale share the stated vertical acceleration while contact persists.
g is the positive magnitude of the downward gravitational acceleration.

relations.meaning: In a one-axis frame accelerating with signed acceleration a_frame relative to an inertial frame, the pseudo-force assigned to a mass m is opposite the frame acceleration and has magnitude m|a_frame|.

symbols.meaning: Signed pseudo-force used only in the accelerating-frame description
Mass of the described body
Signed acceleration of the selected non-inertial frame relative to the inertial frame

conditions: The selected observer frame has nonzero translational acceleration relative to the inertial frame.
F_pseudo and a_frame use the same declared axis and sign convention.
The mass is positive and treated as constant.
The pseudo-force is a frame-dependent modelling term, not a physical interaction and not a Newton-third-law partner.

relations.meaning: For a bob stationary relative to a horizontally accelerating vehicle, with a massless string and no other horizontal interaction, the equilibrium string tilt theta from the vertical satisfies tan(theta)=|a_frame|/g in the vehicle frame.

symbols.meaning: Magnitude of the string tilt from the vertical
Magnitude/sign source of the vehicle's horizontal frame acceleration
Positive magnitude of gravitational acceleration

conditions: The bob is stationary relative to the vehicle after transients, so its relative acceleration is zero.
The vehicle has constant horizontal acceleration over the represented state.
The string is massless and taut, and air resistance is neglected.
theta is measured from the vertical; the bob tilts opposite the vehicle acceleration.

validity_conditions: Keep velocity direction separate from acceleration direction; apparent weight depends on acceleration, not on whether the elevator is moving up or down.
Use REL-NLM-ELEVATOR-SUPPORT only while scale contact persists; if the unconstrained calculation would require N < 0, the contact model has failed rather than producing a negative scale reading.
At free fall a_y = -g, the support force is N = 0 while the gravitational force mg remains nonzero.
Use REL-NLM-PSEUDO-FORCE only in the explicitly selected accelerating frame; do not add it in the inertial ground-frame equation.
Dual-frame calculations must describe the same body and physical event and must agree on observable support force/string direction.
Keep this gate as explicit-demand extension content; it does not make R4 a default Grade-9 learner coordinate.

reasoning_sequence.action: Declare the observer frame, its acceleration, and the signed axis before writing any force equation.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Whether a pseudo-force term appears depends on observer acceleration, so frame choice is part of the model.

reasoning_sequence.action: Inventory the physical interactions on the chosen body and keep their forces unchanged when switching observers.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Changing observers does not create or remove physical agents.

reasoning_sequence.action: If the selected frame accelerates, add REL-NLM-PSEUDO-FORCE with direction opposite a_frame; otherwise do not add it.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: The pseudo-force is the declared convention that compensates for the frame acceleration.

reasoning_sequence.action: Compare an observable such as scale reading or string direction across the inertial and accelerating descriptions.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Two consistent descriptions of one physical event must predict the same observable.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A scale always reads mg because weight is mg.
misconceptions.counterexample: In an upward-accelerating elevator N = m(g+a_y) > mg, while in free fall N = 0 even though mg remains nonzero.
misconceptions.repair: Treat the scale reading as the normal/support force and solve the force balance for N.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: An elevator moving upward must make the scale read heavier.
misconceptions.counterexample: An elevator can move upward while accelerating downward and then N < mg.
misconceptions.repair: Use acceleration direction, not velocity direction, in the force equation.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Pseudo-force is a new physical interaction or a third-law partner.
misconceptions.counterexample: The same physical agents are present in the inertial and accelerating descriptions; only the accelerating description introduces the pseudo term.
misconceptions.repair: Name physical agents first, then add the frame term only after selecting a non-inertial observer.

problem_families.title: Apparent weight and contact in a vertically accelerating elevator
hidden_invariants: Scale reading is N, not mg.
Velocity direction does not determine N; acceleration does.
N cannot be negative while the person remains on the floor.

problem_families.title: One event described in inertial and accelerating frames
hidden_invariants: Physical interaction forces are unchanged by observer choice.
The pseudo term appears only in the accelerating-frame bookkeeping.
Observable predictions agree when each frame is used consistently.

difficulty.note: The algebra is short; the main difficulty is choosing the observer, separating velocity from acceleration, and distinguishing physical interactions from a frame-dependent pseudo term.

falsification_cases.mutation: Remove the Physics-required unit field from the first symbol of the elevator relation.

gates.title: Force from discrete momentum transfer per unit time

canonical_concepts.statement: For one fixed-mass item in a declared inertial frame, linear momentum is directed and changes by final minus initial momentum.
Net external force is the directed rate of momentum change for the same chosen system and frame.
For repeated identical item momentum changes, items per unit time times momentum change per item gives the average momentum-transfer force on the stream.

relations.meaning: The signed one-dimensional linear momentum of one fixed-mass item equals its mass times its signed velocity in the declared inertial frame.

symbols.meaning: Signed linear momentum of one item
Positive fixed mass of that item
Signed velocity of the item in the declared inertial frame

conditions: The item mass is positive and fixed during the compared states.
Velocity and momentum use the same declared one-dimensional positive direction.
Initial and final velocities are measured in the same inertial frame.

relations.meaning: The net external force on a chosen system equals its directed rate of change of linear momentum; this bounded Grade-9 extension evaluates that rate through a steady discrete transfer rather than calculus.

symbols.meaning: Signed net external force on the chosen system
Signed linear momentum of the chosen system or stream
Time

conditions: System boundary, inertial frame and positive direction are declared.
The momentum and force refer to the same chosen system and frame.
For the learner route here, the rate is evaluated from repeated finite momentum transfers; no derivative calculation is required.

relations.meaning: If identical fixed-mass items undergo the same signed momentum change and are ejected at steady rate R items per second, the ejecta stream's average momentum-change rate and average force equal R times the momentum change per item.

symbols.meaning: Signed average force on the ejecta stream
Steady number of identical items ejected per unit time
Signed momentum change of one ejected item

conditions: The represented items are identical for the calculation or share the same Delta p_item.
R is the number ejected per unit time over the averaging interval.
Delta p_item uses the same inertial frame and positive direction for every item.
The reported force is an average over the repeated discrete ejections.

validity_conditions: Declare one inertial frame and one positive direction before assigning momentum or force signs.
Use final minus initial momentum for each fixed-mass item; final momentum alone is valid only when the initial momentum is zero in the chosen frame.
Use the discrete rate form only when the represented repeated items share the stated per-item momentum change or an appropriate average has been defined.
Keep the force on the ejecta, the opposite launcher interaction force and an external holding force on distinct bodies/roles.
Do not infer collision-conservation, impulse-integral, rocket-equation or continuously varying-mass machinery from this gate.

reasoning_sequence.action: Choose the inertial frame, positive direction and item initial/final states.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: All later momentum and force signs depend on one consistent directed description.

reasoning_sequence.action: Compute the signed momentum change of one fixed-mass item.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: The repeated stream transfers that per-item change, not merely final momentum.

reasoning_sequence.action: Convert n repeated item changes over Delta t into the average momentum-change rate and force.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Summing n equal changes then dividing by the same interval gives (n/Delta t)Delta p_item = R Delta p_item.

reasoning_sequence.action: Assign opposite launcher recoil and, if held fixed, the external holding force that balances it.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Interaction partners act on different bodies, and a fixed launcher has zero net average force.

reasoning_sequence.action: Verify newton units and a zero-transfer or sign-reversal boundary case.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: A correct momentum-rate force must have force dimensions and respond consistently to direction or zero momentum change.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Use m v_out per item even when v_in is nonzero in the chosen frame.
misconceptions.counterexample: If v_out equals v_in, the item has nonzero momentum but zero momentum change, so this transfer contributes zero force.
misconceptions.repair: Use Delta p_item=m(v_out-v_in).

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The ejecta force and launcher recoil point in the same direction.
misconceptions.counterexample: Forward momentum gained by the ejecta corresponds to an opposite interaction force on the launcher.
misconceptions.repair: Name the body for each force; the launcher interaction partner is opposite, and a holding force balances that recoil.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any ejection-rate problem requires a rocket equation or full variable-mass dynamics.
misconceptions.counterexample: A steady count of identical fixed-mass items can be handled by summing their per-item momentum changes over a finite interval.
misconceptions.repair: Use the bounded repeated-item rate unless the problem explicitly asks for continuous variable-mass evolution.

problem_families.title: Average force from repeated identical momentum changes
hidden_invariants: The same frame, sign convention and per-item momentum change are used throughout the averaging interval.

problem_families.title: Launcher recoil and balancing holding force
hidden_invariants: Force on ejecta, interaction recoil on launcher and external holding force are distinct directed quantities on the appropriate bodies.

difficulty.note: The computation is short; system boundary, final-minus-initial momentum, rate conversion and reaction/holding-force signs are the substantive steps.

gates.title: Grade 9 work, kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy

canonical_concepts.statement: Constant-force work depends on the force component along displacement.
Kinetic energy depends on speed and gravitational potential energy near Earth depends on height relative to a declared reference.
Mechanical energy is conserved only when no additional transfer crosses the chosen mechanical account.
The Grade 9 kinetic- and raised-body potential-energy expressions are consequences of the work ledger plus already-authored force/motion relations, not isolated formulas.

symbols.meaning: Net work by external forces

validity_conditions: Choose the system/account before applying conservation.

reasoning_sequence.action: Choose the body/system, displacement direction and energy reference before selecting a relation.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Work sign and energy values depend on those declarations.

reasoning_sequence.action: Choose work, kinetic energy, potential-energy change, work-energy, or conservation according to the stated transfer and account.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Each relation answers a different bookkeeping question.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any nonzero force on a moving body does positive work.
misconceptions.counterexample: A force perpendicular to displacement has zero along-path component and does zero work.
misconceptions.repair: Resolve force along displacement before multiplying.

gates.title: Grade 9 sound frequency, wavelength, speed and echo relations

canonical_concepts.statement: For one travelling-wave description, propagation speed is frequency times wavelength.
Frequency and time period are reciprocals for one repeating vibration.
An echo delay covers an outward and return sound path, so one-way distance is half the total distance travelled by the sound.

relations.meaning: Wave propagation speed equals temporal frequency times spatial wavelength.

symbols.meaning: Wave propagation speed
Frequency
Wavelength

conditions: f >= 0 and lambda >= 0.
All quantities describe the same wave mode in the same medium/state.

relations.meaning: For a repeating vibration, frequency is the reciprocal of time period.

symbols.meaning: Frequency
Time period

conditions: f and T refer to the same repeating vibration.

relations.meaning: For a single echo from a stationary reflecting surface, one-way source-to-reflector distance is half the sound speed times the measured round-trip echo delay.

symbols.meaning: One-way source-to-reflector distance
Sound speed in the medium
Round-trip echo delay

conditions: t_echo >= 0.
The measured delay is for one outward-and-return path in the same medium.

validity_conditions: Frequency and wavelength refer to the same travelling wave.
Changing medium may change the propagation speed relation through the medium properties.
Period/frequency comparisons refer to one repeating vibration.
Echo distance uses a round-trip delay and therefore includes the factor one half.

reasoning_sequence.action: Identify one frequency and its corresponding wavelength for the same wave.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Mixing values from different waves breaks the relation.

reasoning_sequence.action: Multiply frequency by wavelength to obtain propagation speed.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: One cycle per period advances one wavelength in the travelling-wave description.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Raising source frequency in the same medium must raise wave speed.
misconceptions.counterexample: For a medium-set speed, higher frequency is accompanied by shorter wavelength.
misconceptions.repair: Keep medium and mode fixed before deciding which quantity can change.

problem_families.title: Frequency-wavelength comparisons in one medium
hidden_invariants: If speed is fixed by the medium, frequency and wavelength vary inversely.

falsification_cases.mutation: Remove the Physics-required unit field from the first symbol of the first declared relation.

gates.title: Grade 9 simple machines and mechanical advantage

canonical_concepts.statement: A simple machine can trade force magnitude, direction or input distance; it does not create work or energy.
Mechanical advantage compares load force with effort force for the same machine state.

relations.meaning: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of load force magnitude to effort force magnitude.

symbols.meaning: Mechanical advantage
Load force magnitude
Effort force magnitude

conditions: F_load >= 0.
F_effort > 0.
Load and effort magnitudes refer to the same machine state.

relations.meaning: For an ideal lossless simple machine, input work equals useful output work.

symbols.meaning: Effort force magnitude
Distance moved at the effort point
Load force magnitude
Distance moved by the load

conditions: Ideal lossless model.
Each force magnitude is paired with displacement along its own line of action.
All distances are nonnegative magnitudes.

validity_conditions: State whether the machine is being treated as ideal before equating input and output work.
Mechanical advantage compares force magnitudes, not energies.

reasoning_sequence.action: Identify what the machine changes: effort force, direction, or input distance.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: A machine's benefit is a tradeoff, not new energy.

reasoning_sequence.action: Compare load and effort forces through MA = F_load/F_effort.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: REL-MECHANICAL-ADVANTAGE owns the force ratio.

reasoning_sequence.action: For an ideal machine, connect reduced effort force to increased effort distance through equal input/output work.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: REL-IDEAL-MACHINE-WORK owns the ideal work tradeoff.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A machine with mechanical advantage greater than one creates energy because the output force is larger.
misconceptions.counterexample: An ideal machine that halves effort force requires a correspondingly larger effort distance for the same work.
misconceptions.repair: Track both force and distance; mechanical advantage is a force tradeoff, not an energy gain.

problem_families.title: Lever, pulley and inclined-plane force tradeoffs
hidden_invariants: The same useful load work is compared with the effort work under an explicitly ideal or non-ideal model.

falsification_cases.mutation: Remove the Physics-required unit field from the first symbol of the first declared relation.

gates.title: Grade 10 spherical-mirror image construction, formula and magnification

canonical_concepts.statement: For a spherical mirror in the paraxial model, principal-ray rules are consistent constructions for locating the same image point; image nature follows whether reflected rays or only their backward extensions meet.
For a spherical mirror under one declared Cartesian sign convention and the paraxial approximation, signed object distance u, image distance v and focal length f satisfy 1/v + 1/u = 1/f.
Mirror magnification m = h_i/h_o = -v/u carries both relative image size and orientation; its sign is physically meaningful.

relations.meaning: For one spherical mirror in the paraxial model, signed image distance and object distance combine to the reciprocal signed focal length.

symbols.meaning: Signed object distance measured from the mirror pole
Signed image distance measured from the mirror pole
Signed focal length of the spherical mirror

conditions: u, v and f use the same declared Cartesian sign convention and mirror pole as origin.
The spherical-mirror construction is used in the paraxial/small-angle regime.
u, v and f describe the same mirror and object-image state.

relations.meaning: For the same spherical-mirror image, transverse magnification is the signed image-to-object height ratio and equals negative signed image distance divided by signed object distance.

symbols.meaning: Signed transverse magnification
Signed object distance from the mirror pole
Signed image distance from the mirror pole
Signed image height relative to the principal axis
Signed object height relative to the principal axis

conditions: u, v, h_i and h_o use one declared Cartesian sign convention.
Object and image refer to the same spherical-mirror state.
h_o is nonzero when the height ratio is evaluated.

validity_conditions: Declare the mirror pole, principal axis, incident-light direction and vertical sign convention before assigning signed optical quantities.
Use the spherical-mirror formula only within the paraxial/small-angle model rather than claiming exact convergence for arbitrary wide-aperture rays.
A valid principal-ray pair must locate one common image point or one common backward-extension point.
The sign of magnification is retained because it distinguishes erect from inverted images.

reasoning_sequence.action: Construct at least two valid principal rays from one object point and require a common physical or backward-extension intersection.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: The spherical-mirror image is a geometric property of one reflected ray bundle, not of a chosen decorative ray.

reasoning_sequence.action: Assign u, v and f only after declaring the Cartesian coordinate directions from the pole.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: The mirror equation relates signed coordinates; object/image labels alone do not determine signs.

reasoning_sequence.action: Apply REL-MIRROR-EQUATION to the same paraxial mirror state and cross-check the result against the ray construction.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: The equation and construction are two representations of the same model.

reasoning_sequence.action: Use REL-MIRROR-MAGNIFICATION and retain its sign when predicting relative size and orientation.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Magnitude alone cannot distinguish erect from inverted images.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Principal-ray rules can be mixed arbitrarily even if they predict different image points.
misconceptions.counterexample: Two valid ray rules for the same object point and mirror must intersect at the same image point within the model.
misconceptions.repair: Treat each principal ray as constrained by the same mirror geometry and reject an inconsistent construction.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Object distance, image distance and focal length have permanent signs based only on their labels.
misconceptions.counterexample: Reversing the page drawing while carrying the declared incident-light direction with the physical setup preserves the coordinate rule rather than page-left/page-right mnemonics.
misconceptions.repair: Declare origin and positive directions first, then assign every distance and height sign from those coordinates.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The spherical-mirror formula is exact for arbitrary rays striking anywhere on a wide spherical mirror.
misconceptions.counterexample: Large-angle rays far from the principal axis need not converge to the single point predicted by the paraxial approximation.
misconceptions.repair: State the paraxial model before using the formula and treat wide-aperture disagreement as a model-limit issue.

problem_families.title: Spherical-mirror image construction, signed formula and magnification
hidden_invariants: Ray construction, signed mirror equation and magnification must describe the same object-mirror-image state.
The coordinate convention is declared before substitution.
The paraxial model boundary remains visible when a formula is used.

falsification_cases.mutation: Remove the Physics-required unit field from a mirror-relation symbol.

gates.title: Grade 10 refraction, spherical-lens imaging, magnification and power

canonical_concepts.statement: Refraction angles are measured from the surface normal; across a boundary the ray direction changes because light speed differs between media, while the incident ray, normal and refracted ray remain coplanar.

For the same pair of transparent media and wavelength, n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r); refractive index also expresses the ratio of light speeds, so the angle relation is a model of speed change rather than a drawing mnemonic.
For a thin spherical lens in the paraxial model, independent principal-ray rules must locate the same image point or common backward-extension point.
For a thin spherical lens under one declared Cartesian sign convention and the paraxial approximation, signed object distance u, image distance v and focal length f satisfy 1/v - 1/u = 1/f.
Lens magnification m = h_i/h_o = v/u carries both relative image size and orientation; its sign is physically meaningful.
Lens power P = 1/f when focal length is expressed in metres; power is in dioptres and retains the focal-length sign, so converging and diverging lenses have opposite signs.

relations.meaning: At one planar interface between two transparent media, the normal-referenced incidence and refraction angles are related by the refractive indices of the two media.

symbols.meaning: Refractive index of the incident medium
Refractive index of the refracting medium
Angle of incidence measured from the normal
Angle of refraction measured from the normal

conditions: Angles i and r are measured from the same surface normal at the boundary.
The media and wavelength remain fixed while the angle relation is used.
The incident ray, normal and refracted ray are coplanar.

relations.meaning: Absolute refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium.

symbols.meaning: Absolute refractive index of the medium
Speed of light in vacuum
Speed of light in the medium

conditions: c and v refer to the same light frequency/wavelength context for the stated medium.
v is positive and not greater than c in the ordinary transparent-media model used here.

relations.meaning: For one thin spherical lens in the paraxial model, signed image distance minus signed object-distance reciprocal equals reciprocal signed focal length.

symbols.meaning: Signed object distance from the optical centre
Signed image distance from the optical centre
Signed focal length of the thin lens

conditions: u, v and f use the same declared Cartesian sign convention and optical centre as origin.
The lens is treated as thin and the construction is paraxial/small-angle.
u, v and f describe the same lens and object-image state.

relations.meaning: For the same thin-lens image, transverse magnification is the signed image-to-object height ratio and equals signed image distance divided by signed object distance.

symbols.meaning: Signed transverse magnification
Signed object distance from the optical centre
Signed image distance from the optical centre
Signed image height relative to the principal axis
Signed object height relative to the principal axis

conditions: u, v, h_i and h_o use one declared Cartesian sign convention.
Object and image refer to the same thin-lens state.
h_o is nonzero when the height ratio is evaluated.

relations.meaning: Optical power is the reciprocal focal length when focal length is expressed in metres.

symbols.meaning: Signed optical power of the lens
Signed focal length of the lens

conditions: Focal length f is expressed in metres before taking the reciprocal.
The sign of f is retained, so converging and diverging lens powers have opposite signs.

validity_conditions: Draw the interface or principal axis and the relevant normal/optical centre before assigning angles or signed distances.
Use Snell's law with angles measured from the normal, never from the interface surface.
Use the spherical-lens equation only within the thin-lens, paraxial/small-angle model.
A valid principal-ray pair must locate one common physical or backward-extension image point.
Retain the signs of lens magnification and focal length because orientation and converging/diverging character depend on them.
Convert focal length to metres before computing power in dioptres.

reasoning_sequence.action: Draw the normal at the boundary, label the media, and determine whether the ray bends toward or away from the normal from the refractive-index comparison.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: Refraction is defined relative to the local normal and a speed/index change, not the page edge.

reasoning_sequence.action: Use REL-SNELLS-LAW and, when required, REL-REFRACTIVE-INDEX-SPEED to connect measured angles and material index.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: The two relations connect ray geometry to the physical speed change.

reasoning_sequence.action: Construct at least two valid principal rays for one thin lens and require a common image or backward-extension intersection.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: The image belongs to one refracted ray bundle rather than to a memorized diagram.

reasoning_sequence.action: Declare the Cartesian signs, apply REL-LENS-EQUATION to the same paraxial lens state, and cross-check its image region against the ray construction.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: The equation and ray construction are representations of the same thin-lens model.

reasoning_sequence.action: Use REL-LENS-MAGNIFICATION and retain its sign when interpreting relative size and orientation.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: An unsigned size ratio cannot distinguish erect from inverted images.

reasoning_sequence.action: Convert focal length to metres and use REL-LENS-POWER, retaining focal-length sign.
reasoning_sequence.why_valid: The dioptre is inverse metre and the sign distinguishes converging from diverging lenses.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Refraction angles are measured from the interface surface.
misconceptions.counterexample: A ray travelling along the normal has incidence and refraction angles of zero, not ninety degrees.
misconceptions.repair: Draw the normal first and measure both angles from it.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The mirror relation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f can be copied unchanged for a lens.
misconceptions.counterexample: The governed thin-lens relation is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f under the declared Cartesian convention.
misconceptions.repair: Identify reflection versus refraction first, then use the relation owned by that optical model.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A focal length written in centimetres can be substituted directly into P = 1/f to obtain dioptres.
misconceptions.counterexample: A 50 cm converging lens has f = 0.50 m and P = +2 D, not +0.02 D.
misconceptions.repair: Convert f to metres and retain its sign before taking the reciprocal.

problem_families.title: Normal-based refraction, thin-lens imaging, signed formula, magnification and power
hidden_invariants: Angles are measured from the normal and indices belong to the declared media.
Ray construction, signed lens equation and magnification describe the same lens state.
Thin-lens/paraxial validity remains visible when a lens formula is used.
Power uses focal length in metres and retains its sign.

falsification_cases.mutation: Remove the Physics-required unit field from a lens/refraction relation symbol.
